direct_answer:
Motoroil (MOTOR OIL Group) conducted its double materiality assessment (DMA) as a structured, multi-step process to identify, reassess and prioritise sustainability topics under both (i) impact materiality (effects on society, governance and the environment) and (ii) financial materiality (risks/opportunities that affect or could reasonably be expected to affect financial position/performance, cash flows, access to funding or cost of capital across short-, medium- and long-term horizons) [Source 4].

How the DMA was conducted:
- Inventory creation: built an initial inventory of impacts, risks and opportunities via (a) sub-topic analysis, (b) benchmarking against peers, (c) review of previously identified material topics, and (d) review of sector-specific CSRD standards; with particular focus on high-impact activities/business relationships (e.g., refining, energy infrastructure, petrochemicals; hazardous materials; high energy intensity; land use) and geographies with elevated environmental/social risks [Source 4].
- Value chain and due diligence integration: performed value chain analysis across upstream, own operations and downstream (sourcing, production, distribution, product end-use) to assess where impacts are most likely and to evaluate severity and likelihood across stages; own operations and downstream were identified as primary areas of material impact (especially environmental and safety), while some upstream social risks (e.g., human rights/child labour) were assessed as less likely/severe due to indirect involvement but still addressed via due diligence measures (e.g., Supplier Code of Conduct) [Source 12]. The impact identification/assessment process is described as closely integrated with the Group’s sustainability due diligence framework [Source 12].
- Stakeholder mapping and engagement: developed a stakeholder map distinguishing affected stakeholders and users of sustainability statements; used engagement methods such as communication channels, workshops and feedback mechanisms; assigned priority levels to stakeholder groups to inform engagement resourcing and integrate stakeholder perspectives into decision-making [Source 10]. Stakeholder Representatives conducted structured dialogues/meetings/consultations and a Third Party was appointed to collect/analyse feedback and support objective representation of stakeholder input in scoring [Source 11].
- Validation and governance oversight: Sustainability Division validated wording/categorisation of IROs and used cross-functional dialogue with relevant departments where needed [Source 6]. Management validation included review by the Sustainability Committee to ensure robustness and strategic alignment [Source 1]. The Sustainability Committee (Board members) approved the DMA process and scoring results; the Board of Directors held ultimate accountability and integrated DMA findings into strategy, capital allocation and major approvals; the Audit Committee oversaw integrity/completeness of disclosures [Source 5, Source 15, Source 8].
- Scoring methodology (impact and financial): impact materiality scoring assessed impacts on external stakeholders (communities, employees, customers, environment) using Scale, Scope, Irreversibility and Likelihood (for potential impacts), and considered time horizons [Source 2]. Financial materiality scoring assessed likelihood and financial effect using Magnitude and Likelihood, also considering time horizons; the Risk Management Unit guided risk identification and likelihood/financial effect scoring, while the Group Strategy General Directorate supported opportunity evaluation including financial projections and cost-benefit analyses [Source 2]. The Group also explicitly considered dependencies on natural and human capital across the value chain when evaluating significance [Source 7].
- Integration into ERM: financial materiality was integrated into the broader DMA framework with support from an external consultant and coordinated with the Risk Management Unit; sustainability risks/opportunities were aligned with overall risk management strategy and captured in a Risk Register; the assessment included qualitative and quantitative evaluation of potential financial losses and benefits [Source 1].

Which sustainability matters were identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective:
- The retrieved passages do not list the specific sustainability matters/topics that are material in both dimensions. They only provide aggregate counts: the Group evaluated 38 sustainability-related impacts and assessed 27 as material (13 Environmental, 9 Social, 3 Governance, plus 2 entity-specific impacts), and identified 41 sustainability-related risks and opportunities with 28 considered material (14 Environmental, 9 Social, 3 Governance) [Source 9]. Therefore, based on the provided evidence, it is not possible to identify which specific sustainability matters were material from both an impact and a financial perspective.
compliance_rationale: The company discloses substantial information on how it conducted the DMA, including inventory building, value chain focus, stakeholder mapping/engagement (including third-party support), validation, scoring criteria for impact and financial materiality, governance oversight, and integration into ERM/risk register with qualitative and quantitative evaluation [Source 1, Source 2, Source 4, Source 6, Source 10, Source 11, Source 12]. However, the retrieved passages do not disclose the specific sustainability matters that are material in both impact and financial terms; only aggregate counts by E/S/G are provided [Source 9].
disclosure_gaps: List of specific sustainability matters/topics identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective (intersection of the two dimensions) is not provided in the retrieved passages [Source 9].

Explicit thresholds/decision rules (“thresholding”) used to determine material vs non-material are not included in the retrieved passages (the section heading appears but content is not shown) [Source 10].
Clear mapping from identified IROs to ESRS sustainability matters (and which matters are material due to impact, financial, or both) is not evidenced in the retrieved passages [Source 9].

Disclosure of interdependencies between impact and financial materiality outcomes (e.g., how impact materiality informed financial materiality and vice versa) is described generally but not shown as an explicit linkage per matter/topic [Source 1, Source 4].
key_findings: Motoroil conducted a DMA covering both impact materiality and financial materiality, explicitly referencing financial effects on financial position/performance, cash flows, access to funding and cost of capital across time horizons [Source 4].
The DMA inventory was built using peer benchmarking, review of prior material topics, and sector-specific CSRD standards, with focus on high-impact activities and business relationships [Source 4].

The assessment was integrated with due diligence and included value chain mapping across upstream/own operations/downstream; own operations and downstream were identified as primary areas of material impact, particularly environmental and safety [Source 12].

Stakeholder mapping and engagement were used to integrate stakeholder perspectives; Stakeholder Representatives and a Third Party supported structured engagement and objective incorporation into scoring [Source 10, Source 11].

Impact scoring used Scale, Scope, Irreversibility and Likelihood (for potential impacts) and time horizons; financial scoring used Magnitude and Likelihood and time horizons, with Risk Management and Strategy functions supporting scoring [Source 2].
Financial materiality was integrated into ERM with qualitative and quantitative evaluation and use of a Risk Register [Source 1].
The report provides only aggregate counts of material impacts and material risks/opportunities by E/S/G category, not the specific matters material in both dimensions [Source 9].
